newsitem.title: USA: White House to give agencies' views of EPA air plan.
newsitem.headline: White House to give agencies' views of EPA air plan.

text.p: The Clinton administration, under fire to disclose its own top officials' concerns over a plan to tighten air quality standards, said on Friday its agencies will be encouraged to offer their views of the plan.

"We are involved in an inter-agency process that is encouraging agencies to comment, and we will make that public," said an official with the Environmental Protection Agency, which proposed the controversial new standards against smog and soot pollution.

West Virginia Sen. Robert Byrd on Thursday charged that the White House's Office of Management and Budget had tried to suppress criticisms of the air standards plan leveled by agencies such as the Transportation Department and the Small Business Administration.

The senior Democrat asked federal agencies -- some of whom had rapped the EPA plan in an internal review -- to gauge the new standards' costs on their own operations and on the industry sectors they regulate.
Byrd also called on the OMB to give its own estimate of the new standards' overall costs to the federal government.
"The EPA and OMB should step out into the sunshine and share with the public all of the comments from federal agencies," Byrd said in a statement.

Earlier this month, he and four other Democrats from eastern coal-producing states broke party ranks and urged the EPA to delay the new standards that could reduce demand for the kind of dirty, high-sulfur coal their region produces.
The EPA has estimated that meeting the new standards would cost $6.5 billion to $8.5 billion annually, but said new technology could bring those costs down.
But in internal comments submitted before the EPA announced its plan, several agencies disputed those estimates and urged the agency to reconsider its proposal.
Industry groups opposed to the new standards released the internal administration memos.

A member of the president's Council of Economic Advisers, Alicia Munnell, said the council's estimates put costs as high as $60 billion. Her memo said the "incremental health-risk reduction for more stringent air standards is small, while costs are high."

The Transportation Department urged the EPA to rethink its plan, saying, "Control measures needed to meet the standards could have significant economic impacts on industry, including previously unregulated business, and require lifestyle changes by a significant part of the U.S. population."
The Small Business Administration said the rule "would be a startling proposition to the small business community," and suggested the EPA "reconsider the stringency of the proposal."
EPA Administrator Carol Browner has staunchly defended the proposal, saying scientific evidence showed that current standards do not adequately protect public health.
